questions.q: Define entropy and state its SI unit. Is entropy a state function or a path function? Justify your answer in one sentence.
questions.a: Entropy (S) is a measure of disorder or randomness in a system; its SI unit is J K⁻¹. It is a state function because its value depends only on the initial and final states of the system, not on the path taken. A wrong answer (e.g., "entropy is heat" or "unit is J/mol") reveals confusion between heat (path function) and entropy (state function), or missing the temperature denominator in the definition.

questions.q: Explain why the entropy change for melting of 1 mol of ice at 0 °C and 1 atm is positive, even though the temperature of the system remains constant during the phase change.
questions.a: Melting requires absorption of latent heat (q_rev = ΔH_fus > 0) at constant T = 273 K, so ΔS_sys = ΔH_fus/T > 0. The molecular randomness increases as ordered solid water becomes disordered liquid. A wrong answer (e.g., "ΔS = 0 because T is constant") reveals the misconception that entropy change depends only on temperature change, ignoring the heat transfer at constant T.

questions.q: Calculate the entropy change when 36 g of water vaporizes at its boiling point (373 K) and 1 atm. Given: ΔH_vap = 40.7 kJ mol⁻¹. (Molar mass of water = 18 g mol⁻¹)
questions.a:
Step 1: Moles of water = 36 g / 18 g mol⁻¹ = 2 mol.
Step 2: Heat absorbed reversibly = 2 mol × 40.7 kJ mol⁻¹ = 81.4 kJ = 81400 J.
Step 3: ΔS = q_rev/T = 81400 J / 373 K = 218.2 J K⁻¹.
A wrong answer (e.g., forgetting to convert kJ to J, or using mass instead of moles) reveals unit inconsistency or not recognizing that ΔH_vap is per mole.

questions.q: A system undergoes an irreversible adiabatic expansion into vacuum (free expansion). Compare the entropy change of the system, surroundings, and universe for this process with those for a reversible adiabatic expansion between the same initial and final states.
questions.a: Free expansion: q = 0, so ΔS_surr = 0. But process is irreversible, so ΔS_sys > 0 (calculated via a reversible path), hence ΔS_univ > 0. Reversible adiabatic: q_rev = 0, so ΔS_sys = 0, ΔS_surr = 0, ΔS_univ = 0. A wrong answer (e.g., "ΔS_sys = 0 for free expansion because q = 0") reveals the misconception that ΔS = q/T for irreversible paths; entropy is a state function so we must use a reversible path to calculate ΔS_sys.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "For an exothermic reaction at constant T and P, the entropy change of the surroundings is always positive, so the reaction is always spontaneous." Identify the error and correct it.
questions.a: The statement is partially correct that ΔS_surr = -ΔH_sys/T > 0 for exothermic reactions, but spontaneity requires ΔS_univ = ΔS_sys + ΔS_surr > 0. If ΔS_sys is sufficiently negative, ΔS_univ could be negative. The error is ignoring the system's entropy change. A wrong evaluation (e.g., agreeing with the statement) reveals the misconception that only surroundings' entropy matters, or that exothermic always means spontaneous.

questions.q: Design a simple experiment using two gases (e.g., NO₂ and N₂O₄) to demonstrate that a spontaneous process increases the entropy of the universe. Describe what you would observe and how it relates to ΔS_univ > 0.
questions.a: Place brown NO₂ gas in a sealed syringe at room temperature; it partially dimerizes to colourless N₂O₄ (2NO₂ ⇌ N₂O₄). Compress the syringe: colour fades (forward reaction, fewer gas moles). Release: colour darkens (reverse reaction, more gas moles). Both directions occur spontaneously depending on pressure, each increasing total entropy (system + surroundings) by dispersing energy/matter. A poor answer (e.g., only describing colour change without linking to entropy) reveals inability to connect macroscopic observation to the Second Law.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Entropy (S) is a ______ state function that quantifies the degree of disorder or randomness in a system; for a reversible process at constant temperature, the entropy change is defined as ΔS = q_rev/T, where q_rev is the heat absorbed reversibly and T is the absolute temperature.

Fill in the blank: Start with a real-world observation: when you open a bottle of perfume in a corner of a room, the fragrance spreads everywhere on its own — but it never ______ collects back into the bottle.
What is Entropy (S)? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Entropy (S) is a thermodynamic state function that quantifies the degree of disorder or randomness in a system; for a reversible process at constant temperature, the entropy change is defined as ΔS = q_rev/T, where q_rev is the heat absorbed reversibly and T is the absolute temperature.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Ask students: "What drives this one-way spreading?" Connect to prior concept of energy conservation (First Law, node ______) which cannot explain directionality.
What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Entropy (S)?
questions.a: Students often write ΔS = q/T for any process, forgetting that this formula is valid ONLY for reversible paths.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to calculate entropy change for phase transitions and temperature changes using ΔS = q_rev/T, determine spontaneity by evaluating ΔS_universe = ΔS_sys + ΔS_surr, and explain why entropy increases in irreversible processes like free expansion or mixing of gases.
